## Why this unit matters

Give Product two instances and decide where each request should go. Compare client-side versus proxy-side routing, then study the course's Ribbon implementation.

The same shop remains the anchor: Product owns catalogue information, User owns customer information, and Order coordinates checkout. Read each chapter in order to see which new requirement motivates the next design decision.

## Lessons

1. **[Client-side and Server-side Load Balancing](client-server-balancing.qmd)**
2. **[Netflix Ribbon: Usage and Strategies](ribbon-usage.qmd)**
3. **[Ribbon: Internal Workflow](ribbon-internals.qmd)**

## Learning objective

After this unit, describe the dependency or operational problem **before** naming a framework; draw the relevant call/event path; state the failure mode and trade-off; and explain how the concept applies to a small TypeScript or NestJS service.

## Source mapping and example

**Supplied source:** Day 1 §6–7. The content is an original explanation of the supplied course's topics and not a reproduction of its Java code. Start the [single-file Node.js shop lab](../examples/README.md) to inspect the related HTTP endpoints. Framework-specific components that are not present in the lab are explained as architectural patterns.

## Mathematical Abstraction

A selector maps a request and current candidates to one instance.

$$
b:(r,D_t(s))\mapsto i,\quad i\in D_t(s)
$$

$b$ is the load-balancer rule; the chosen instance may fail before the request arrives.
